vignette:
Ravi is a 26-year-old editor who works from home in a quiet suburban apartment, married for just over a year to a woman he met during graduate school. Eight months ago, he was pulled over late at night on his way back from a late shift at the publishing house. What began as a routine traffic stop escalated without warning. The officer, a large man with a cold, deliberate voice, ordered Ravi out of the car, forced him to the ground, and pressed a knee into his back while shouting commands Ravi could not process. The asphalt was freezing against his cheek, and the officer’s weight made it impossible to breathe. For several minutes, Ravi believed he was going to die. He could smell the officer’s sweat and the exhaust from the patrol car, and even now, when he recalls the event, that same acrid smell returns unbidden — a sharp, chemical odor that makes his stomach turn. When the memories come, and they come often, his body locks into the same position: face down, arms twisted behind him, chest pressed flat. It is not a memory he watches; it is a memory he inhabits. And with it comes a wave of grief so profound that he sometimes finds himself weeping without knowing why, mourning something he cannot name — perhaps the person he used to be, or the world he used to trust.

In the weeks that followed, Ravi began to interpret his reactions as evidence of a fundamental weakness. He could not stop thinking about the event, could not move past it, and he told himself that a stronger person — a better coper — would have shaken it off by now. This belief took root and spread. Nothing in his life felt meaningful anymore; his work, which he had once loved, now seemed hollow. He became certain that nothing good could happen to him again. These appraisals did not remain abstract. They shaped what he noticed and what he feared. He began to monitor his own body for the first flicker of dissociation — that strange, floating sense of unreality that sometimes preceded a full memory intrusion. And he became acutely sensitive to temperature on his skin. A cold draft from an open window, the shock of a cool glass against his palm, the chill of a marble countertop — each could send him reeling, pulling him back to that freezing asphalt. What frightened him most was being alone with women. The officer had been male, but in the months since the incident, Ravi found himself avoiding any situation where he might be alone with a female colleague, friend, or even his wife’s sister. He could not explain why, but the thought of it made his chest tighten, his breath shorten, and his mind begin to drift toward that dissociative fog. Each time he felt that detachment beginning, he told himself he was falling apart, that he was a lousy coper, and that he would never recover.

The cycle tightened. The more he believed he was broken, the more he recalled the event with vivid, bodily clarity. And the more he recalled it, the more he confirmed to himself that his life had lost all meaning. His wife noticed him pulling away. When she asked what was wrong, he said he was tired. He stopped editing manuscripts that dealt with violence or crime, claiming a conflict of interest, and began turning down assignments that required evening deadlines — a quiet, professional retreat that his manager attributed to burnout. He stopped visiting his parents, because their home was cold and he knew the temperature would trigger him. He stopped going to the grocery store alone, because a young woman in the aisle might speak to him and he would feel that familiar, terrifying drift. By the time he sought help, he had not left the apartment in ten days. He came because his wife told him she could not watch him disappear anymore. What he was most afraid of, he said, was that she was right — that there was nothing left to save.
